Six EE Projects That
Put You on a Drone Team

A flight controller from an IMU and a PID loop. An ESC you built from six MOSFETs. A
telemetry link that survives 2 km of open air. A gimbal that holds a horizon, a
power module that reports every cell, and an indoor positioning grid for when GPS is
gone. Six benches, six flight-ready builds, one portfolio a drone company will
actually read.

01
Flight controller from scratch
write your own attitude filter and PID loop on an ESP32 + MPU6050 and balance a
one-axis rig before you ever spin four props.

02
Brushless ESC you built
drive a 3-phase motor with six MOSFETs and back-EMF commutation on a board you laid
out yourself — the part every drone company buys in.

03
LoRa telemetry link
stream GPS, altitude and battery voltage from the airframe to a ground station 2 km
away on a 915 MHz LoRa link you budgeted yourself.

04
Brushless camera gimbal
hold a camera level through pitch and roll with two gimbal motors, an IMU on the
camera plate and your own sine-wave drive.

05
Smart battery power module
read every cell voltage, pack current and mAh used on a 4S LiPo with your own shunt
amplifier, and warn the pilot before the pack sags.

06
GPS-denied indoor positioning
place three UWB anchors around a room and trilaterate a tag on the drone to ±10 cm —
how warehouse drones fly where GPS can't reach.

●

❯project 01
Flight controller from scratch

write your own attitude filter and PID loop on an ESP32 + MPU6050 and balance a one-axis
rig before you ever spin four props.

$18
intermediate
2 weekends
## why this matters

Every drone company assumes a graduate has only ever flashed Betaflight, and that assumption
is usually correct. This project forces you through the part the firmware hides: raw gyro
rates and accelerometer vectors coming in at 1 kHz, a complementary (or Kalman) filter turning
them into a roll and pitch angle, and a PID loop turning that angle error into motor commands.
You will discover that the textbook loop oscillates on a real rig, that the gyro drifts, that
the accelerometer lies under vibration, and that the difference between a stable hover and a
flip is a derivative term and a 100 Hz low-pass filter. Debugging that on a hinged one-axis
test stand, with a logged plot of setpoint versus measured angle, is the actual skill a
flight-controls engineer is hired for.
WHAT THIS PROVES TO A RECRUITER

You can explain where your angle estimate comes from, why you fused gyro and
accelerometer instead of trusting either, what your loop rate is and why, and what the
D-term does when the motor response is slow. You tuned gains on real hardware with a
logged step response, not a slider in a simulator. That is a control-systems story a
drone company can check in one question — and almost no one walks in with it.
→ the job this maps to: Flight controls / GNC engineer — attitude estimation and inner-loop
stabilization for multirotors.
SAFETY WARNING

Run every test with propellers removed until the rig is stable on the stand; a loop that
saturates will spin motors to full throttle without warning.
## how it works
▸ Two sensors, two failure modes: the gyro gives clean rate but integrates into drift; the

accelerometer gives an absolute tilt but is swamped by motor vibration — the filter trusts
the gyro fast and the accelerometer slow.
▸ Loop rate sets the ceiling: a 250 Hz loop can stabilize a rig whose dynamics are 10–20 Hz;
go slower and the phase lag alone will make a well-tuned loop oscillate.
▸ Derivative on measurement, not error: putting D on the error makes every setpoint step a
spike to the motors; on the measurement it only reacts to what the rig is actually doing.
▸ Motor response is part of the plant: a brushless motor plus ESC has 30–80 ms of lag, which
is why the same gains that work in simulation oscillate on the bench.
▸ A test stand is not a cheat: every real flight-controller team tunes inner loops on a
constrained rig first — crashing a rig costs nothing, crashing an airframe costs a week.

## key design decisions
→ Why a complementary filter instead of a full Kalman filter?: at this sensor quality the

complementary filter is within a degree of an EKF on roll and pitch and fits in ten lines
you can defend at a whiteboard; the EKF is the right answer once you add a magnetometer and
GPS.
→ Why an ESP32 instead of an Arduino Uno?: the Uno's 16 MHz 8-bit core struggles to hold 250

Hz with floating-point math; the ESP32 runs the loop at 1 kHz with headroom and has a
second core for logging.
→ Why a one-axis rig instead of tethering the quad?: a tether still lets the aircraft couple
roll, pitch and yaw, so you cannot tell which gain is wrong; one axis, one loop, one plot.

## build steps

1
Step 1

Wire the MPU6050 to the ESP32 over I2C at 400 kHz, set the gyro to ±500 °/s and accel to
±4 g, and log raw readings at 1 kHz to confirm you actually get 1000 samples a second
before you write any control code.

2
Build the one-axis test stand

a 2 mm carbon rod through a 3D-printed cradle holding two motor arms, so the rig can only
roll — one degree of freedom means one PID loop to tune, not three.

3
Step 3

Implement the complementary filter (angle = 0.98·(angle + gyro·dt) + 0.02·accel_angle)
and plot the output against a protractor at 0°, 15° and 30° before trusting it.

4
Step 4

Write the PID loop at 250 Hz with the D-term on the measurement (not the error) and a 100
Hz first-order filter on it, then tune P first until the rig just oscillates, add D until
it settles, add I last to remove the standing offset.

5
Step 5

Log setpoint, measured angle and motor output to a CSV over serial, do a 20° step and
keep the plot — rise time, overshoot and settling time are the numbers you will be asked
for.
## interview questions
→ Why can't you just integrate the gyro to get the angle?
→ What loop rate did you run and how did you choose it?
→ What happens to your loop if the ESC adds 50 ms of lag?
→ Why is the D-term on the measurement instead of the error?
→ Show me the step response — what is the overshoot and why?

❯project 02
Brushless ESC you built

drive a 3-phase motor with six MOSFETs and back-EMF commutation on a board you laid out
yourself — the part every drone company buys in.

$14
advanced
2 weekends
## why this matters

An ESC is a black box to most EE students: a $12 brick that turns a PWM signal into a spinning
motor. Inside it is a three-phase half-bridge, gate drivers, a microcontroller and a way of
finding the rotor without sensors — by watching the back-EMF zero crossing on the floating
phase. Building it yourself means you will blow a MOSFET by shooting through a half-bridge,
you will see the back-EMF on a scope and learn why it only appears once the motor is already
turning, and you will write an open-loop start-up ramp that hands off to sensorless
commutation. That is the exact circuit inside every motor controller in the industry, and the
debugging — dead time, gate charge, current spikes — is the actual job.
WHAT THIS PROVES TO A RECRUITER

You can draw a three-phase bridge from memory, explain dead-time and shoot-through,
describe how zero-crossing detection works and why it fails at low speed, and show a
scope capture of your own commutation. Motor-drive engineers are among the hardest hires
in the drone and EV world; a working board you laid out puts you in a different pile.
→ the job this maps to: Motor drive / power electronics engineer — ESC and inverter design for
propulsion.
## how it works
▸ Six switches, one rule: at any instant one high-side and one low-side MOSFET on different
phases are on, the third phase floats — that floating phase is where you read the back-EMF.
▸ Dead time is not optional: a high-side and low-side on the same leg overlapping for even 100

ns is a short across the battery; the gate driver's delay plus the MOSFET's turn-off sets
it.
▸ Back-EMF needs speed: the floating phase's voltage is proportional to RPM, so below a few
hundred RPM there is nothing to detect — hence the forced open-loop start.
▸ The bootstrap cap is the usual bug: high-side gates are driven from a capacitor recharged
only when the low side is on, so 100 % duty cycle starves it and the high-side drops out.
▸ Current is the thing that kills boards: a stalled motor draws locked-rotor current; the
shunt and a fast comparator trip is what production ESCs do, and why they survive.
BUILD NOTE

Keep a 2 A current limit on the bench supply and a bulk 470 µF electrolytic right at the
bridge — the first spin-up without it will reboot the MCU on the voltage dip.
## key design decisions

flight control · motor drive · rf links · power — a Build List field guide
5 / 20
→ Why sensorless back-EMF instead of Hall sensors?: drone motors ship without sensors and

every commercial ESC is sensorless; Hall sensors are easier but teach you the wrong
product.
→ Why discrete gate drivers instead of an integrated 3-phase driver IC?: the IR2101 makes each

half-bridge visible on the scope, so you debug dead-time and bootstrap yourself; integrated
drivers like the DRV8302 hide exactly the parts you need to learn.
→ Why a 2-layer board instead of a breadboard?: 15 A switching at 20 kHz on jumper wires

rings, heats and fails; a tight bridge layout with a solid ground pour is the difference
between a spike and a working switch node.

## build steps

1
Design the power stage

three half-bridges of N-channel MOSFETs (e.g. IRLR7843, 30 V, 3 m�) driven by three
IR2101 half-bridge gate drivers with a bootstrap cap and 10 � gate resistors, and lay it
out with the bridge on one side and the MCU on the other.

2
Step 2

Before any motor, test one half-bridge into a resistor load at 12 V with 1 µs dead time
and scope the switch node — a clean edge with no overshoot spike means the gate drive and
layout are right.

3
Step 3

Write the six-step commutation table and spin the motor open-loop with a slow forced ramp
(like a stepper), props off, at low duty — this proves the bridge and the phase order.

4
Add back-EMF sensing

a resistor divider on each phase into the MCU comparator, detect the zero crossing on the
floating phase, wait 30 electrical degrees, then commutate — and log the RPM it locks in
at.

5
Close the loop

ramp open-loop for 0.5 s, hand off to sensorless, then add a throttle input from PWM and
a current shunt so the board shuts down above 15 A.

❯project 03
LoRa telemetry link

stream GPS, altitude and battery voltage from the airframe to a ground station 2 km away
on a 915 MHz LoRa link you budgeted yourself.

$22
intermediate
1-2 weekends
## why this matters

Every drone beyond toy range needs a telemetry downlink, and every drone company has an RF
person who owns it. This project gives you the whole chain: a GPS module and a LoRa radio on
the airframe, a matching radio on a ground station, a packet format you designed, and a range
test you actually ran. You will learn why LoRa trades bit rate for sensitivity, what a link
budget is when you compute it from transmit power, antenna gain and receiver sensitivity, and
why the first range test fails at 300 m because the antenna is lying flat against a carbon
arm. The logged RSSI-versus-distance plot from a walk test is the kind of evidence an RF
hiring manager reads in five seconds.
WHAT THIS PROVES TO A RECRUITER

You can state your link budget with numbers — +20 dBm out, -137 dBm sensitivity at SF12,
2 dBi antennas — and explain what the margin means, why you chose the spreading factor
you did, and how you traded packet rate against range. You ran a walk test and have the
RSSI plot. That is an RF systems story, not a 'used a LoRa library' story.
→ the job this maps to: RF / datalink engineer — telemetry, command-and-control links and
range testing for UAS.
## how it works
▸ Spreading factor is the knob: each step up in SF roughly doubles time-on-air and buys ~2.5
dB of sensitivity — SF7 is fast and short-range, SF12 is slow and long-range.
▸ Link budget is arithmetic, not magic: 20 dBm + 2 dBi + 2 dBi − 97.5 dB (2 km free-space at

915 MHz) = −73.5 dBm at the receiver, against −130 dBm sensitivity — the 56 dB margin is
what survives trees, bodies and a bad antenna.
▸ Antenna placement eats margin first: a whip antenna parallel to a carbon arm is detuned and
shadowed; vertical, clear of carbon, on both ends, recovers 10–20 dB for free.
▸ Binary packets, not JSON: time-on-air scales with bytes, and at SF10 a 20-byte packet is
~330 ms while a 120-byte JSON string is ~1.3 s — you cannot send 2 Hz telemetry in ASCII.
▸ Sequence number plus CRC tells the truth: packet loss, not RSSI, is what the pilot actually
cares about; the logger counts gaps in the sequence.
## key design decisions
→ Why LoRa instead of a 2.4 GHz WiFi or nRF24 link?: at the same transmit power LoRa's

processing gain buys 20–30 dB of sensitivity, which is the difference between 200 m and 2
km; WiFi is faster but dies past the car park.

flight control · motor drive · rf links · power — a Build List field guide
8 / 20
→ Why 915 MHz instead of 433 MHz?: shorter antennas for the same gain, more bandwidth in the

band, and better behaved near the 433 MHz RC-control gear already on many airframes — check
your country's ISM band before buying modules.
→ Why a custom binary packet instead of MAVLink?: MAVLink is what production telemetry uses

and you should mention it, but writing your own 20-byte frame teaches you why every byte
costs airtime; MAVLink can be dropped in afterwards.

Step 1

the air side; power from a 5 V BEC and confirm a GPS fix outdoors before anything else.

a second SX1276 on an ESP32 that parses packets and streams them over USB serial to a
laptop plotting position on a map and RSSI over time.

4

margin) for 2 km free-space at SF10/125 kHz, then pick a spreading factor that gives ≥15
dB margin with ≥2 packets per second.

5
Walk test

log RSSI, SNR and packet loss every 100 m to 2 km with the air unit on a pole, keep the
plot, and note where loss starts versus where your budget said it would.

❯project 04
Brushless camera gimbal

hold a camera level through pitch and roll with two gimbal motors, an IMU on the camera
plate and your own sine-wave drive.

$26
intermediate
2 weekends
## why this matters

A gimbal is a control loop you can see working: the camera stays level while you tilt the
handle. Under that are two things a drone company cares about — sinusoidal open-loop drive of
a brushless motor (three PWM sine waves 120° apart, no commutation sensors) and a fast PID
loop closing on an IMU mounted on the camera plate itself. You will learn why the IMU must be
on the payload and not the frame, why a 400 Hz loop with a 20 Hz plant still jitters if your
PWM frequency is audible, and why the motor gets hot at standstill. The result is a two-axis
rig holding a horizon in a video you can post, plus the logged angle error that proves it.
WHAT THIS PROVES TO A RECRUITER

You can explain sinusoidal commutation versus six-step, why a gimbal motor has high pole
count and high resistance, and how the loop behaves when the IMU is on the frame instead
of the camera. You have a video of it holding level and a plot of residual error. That
is a payload/stabilization story — and every inspection, mapping and cinema drone has
one of these on it.
→ the job this maps to: Payload / stabilization engineer — gimbal drive and camera
stabilization systems for UAS.
## how it works
▸ Sinusoidal drive, no feedback needed: three phases fed sin(�), sin(�+120°), sin(�+240°)

create a rotating field; the rotor follows, so the electrical angle you command is the
mechanical position you get.
▸ Gimbal motors are deliberately weak: many turns of thin wire give high torque per amp at
near-zero speed and let you run them at a few hundred mA continuously without burning out.
▸ IMU on the payload, always: the loop must measure what you are stabilizing; an IMU on the
frame tells you the handle moved, not whether the camera did.
▸ PWM above hearing: at 8 kHz the motor sings; at 20–32 kHz it is silent and the current
ripple is lower — pick the frequency your MCU timer can actually hit.
▸ Two axes, two loops, one coupling: large roll angles rotate the pitch axis, so a 3-axis

gimbal needs proper rotation math — two axes is where you learn it without the math
becoming the whole project.
BUILD NOTE

Gimbal motors draw constant current at standstill — if the driver runs hot, lower the
drive voltage or sine amplitude rather than adding a heatsink; 40 % amplitude holds most
small cameras.

flight control · motor drive · rf links · power — a Build List field guide
11 / 20
## key design decisions
→ Why open-loop sinusoidal drive instead of a sensored servo?: a hobby servo has 1° of dead

band and cogs; sine-driven brushless is smooth to a fraction of a degree and is what every
camera gimbal on the market uses.
→ Why an L6234 instead of three discrete half-bridges?: at under 1 A the integrated driver is

cheaper and cleaner and lets you spend the project on the control loop — you already built
the discrete bridge in the ESC project.
→ Why a 400 Hz loop for a 20 Hz plant?: the motor field is set instantly but the camera plate

has inertia; 20× oversampling keeps the phase lag out of the loop and lets the D-term do
its job.

Step 1

Mount two gimbal motors (e.g. 2208, 90 turns, ~10 �) in a two-axis frame — pitch motor
carries the camera plate, roll motor carries the pitch motor — and bolt an MPU6050 to the
camera plate, not the handle.

2
Step 2

Drive each motor with three PWM outputs through an L6234 (or three half-bridges) at 20–32
kHz, generate sine/cosine tables, and verify the motor turns smoothly when you step the
electrical angle — this is open-loop FOC-style drive.

3
Step 3

Read the IMU at 500 Hz, run the complementary filter from the flight-controller project,
and get a stable pitch/roll estimate on the camera plate before closing anything.

4
Close a PID loop per axis at 400 Hz

the error is the camera angle versus level, the output is the electrical angle advance of
that motor; tune P until it holds, D until it stops humming, I last.

5
Step 5

Record a video tilting the handle ±30° while logging camera angle error; the goal is
under ±0.5° steady-state and no visible bounce on a step.

❯project 05
Smart battery power module

read every cell voltage, pack current and mAh used on a 4S LiPo with your own shunt
amplifier, and warn the pilot before the pack sags.

$16
beginner
1 weekend
## why this matters

Batteries decide flight time and batteries cause crashes, so every drone company has someone
who owns the power module. This project is that module: a shunt resistor and current-sense
amplifier for pack current, a resistor-divider per cell into a multiplexed ADC for cell
voltages, and firmware that integrates current into mAh consumed and flags a weak cell. You
will learn why a 0.5 m� shunt needs a 50 V/V amplifier, why the divider ratio matters for ADC
resolution, why cell voltage under load and at rest are different numbers, and why mAh
consumed is a better land-now signal than voltage. The logged discharge curve you produce is
the first thing a battery engineer asks for.
WHAT THIS PROVES TO A RECRUITER

You can explain high-side versus low-side current sensing, size a shunt for a 60 A pack,
talk about coulomb counting versus voltage estimation, and show a discharge curve with a
weak cell visible in it. That is battery-management experience, and 'BMS' shows up in
nearly every drone, EV and robotics hardware posting.
→ the job this maps to: Battery / power systems engineer — BMS, power monitoring and energy
estimation for electric aircraft.
SAFETY WARNING

Never leave a LiPo connected to a discharge load unattended, and stop any test the
moment a cell reads under 3.0 V — over-discharged cells are the ones that catch fire on
the next charge.
## how it works
▸ Shunt plus amplifier is the whole current sensor: V = I·R, and a milliohm shunt keeps the

loss to a few watts at full throttle while a dedicated current-sense amplifier rejects the
common-mode voltage of the pack.
▸ Cell voltages come from differences: each balance tap is measured to ground, then cell n is

tap n minus tap n−1 — which is why ADC resolution and matched dividers matter more the
higher the cell.
▸ Voltage lies under load: a pack at 14.8 V resting can read 13.6 V at full throttle from

internal resistance alone, which is why voltage alarms trip early and coulomb counting is
what real power modules use.
▸ A weak cell hides at rest: all four cells read 4.1 V on the bench and one dips to 3.2 V
under load; per-cell logging under load is how you find it before it ends a flight.

flight control · motor drive · rf links · power — a Build List field guide
14 / 20
▸ mAh used is the honest fuel gauge: integrate current, compare to rated capacity, and land at
80 % — that is exactly the rule ArduPilot and PX4 power modules enforce.
## key design decisions
→ Why a dedicated current-sense amplifier instead of an op-amp?: an INA240 rejects 80 dB of

common-mode voltage and PWM switching noise at the shunt; a generic op-amp divider on a
16.8 V rail gives you millivolts of error on a millivolt signal.
→ Why a 16-bit external ADC instead of the MCU's 12-bit ADC?: 4.2 V per cell through a divider

into 12 bits gives ~5 mV steps; the ADS1115 gives sub-millivolt resolution, which is what
you need to see a cell drift.
→ Why low-side shunt here?: it keeps the amplifier referenced to ground and is how most hobby

power modules are built; high-side sensing is the production answer when the ground path
must stay unbroken — mention both.

## build steps

1
Size the shunt

for 60 A peak and a 75 mV full-scale amplifier input, choose 1 m� (60 mV at 60 A, 3.6 W
peak — use a 2512 current-sense resistor rated 3 W or two in parallel) and an INA240 or

2
Build the cell-voltage stage

a resistor divider from each balance-lead tap (1S…4S) to an ADS1115 16-bit ADC, scaled so
4.2 V per cell lands below 3.3 V full scale, and compute per-cell voltage as the
difference between adjacent taps.

3
Step 3

Calibrate against a bench meter at 0, 5 and 20 A and at three known voltages — store the
slope and offset in flash, not in a comment.

❯project 06
GPS-denied indoor positioning

place three UWB anchors around a room and trilaterate a tag on the drone to ±10 cm — how
warehouse drones fly where GPS can't reach.

$48
advanced
2 weekends
## why this matters

Indoor drones are the fastest-growing part of the industry — warehouse inventory, tunnel and
tank inspection — and none of them have GPS. This project is the answer those teams actually
use: ultra-wideband ranging. Three ESP32 + DW1000 anchors on tripods, one tag on the airframe,
two-way ranging that times a radio pulse round trip to nanoseconds, and trilateration that
turns three distances into an x/y position on a laptop map. You will learn why UWB can range
to centimetres when WiFi cannot, why antenna delay calibration is the whole game, and why
three anchors give you a position but four give you a sanity check. The logged position trace
as you walk a square is proof you can build a localization system, not just call a library.
WHAT THIS PROVES TO A RECRUITER

You can explain two-way ranging and why it cancels clock offset, what limits UWB
accuracy indoors (antenna delay, multipath, geometry), how trilateration degrades when
anchors are nearly collinear, and you have a plot of a walked square that looks like a
square. Localization and sensor fusion are exactly what indoor-drone companies screen
for — and this build is the first rung of it.
→ the job this maps to: Localization / navigation engineer — GPS-denied positioning and sensor
fusion for indoor UAS.
## how it works
▸ Time of flight, not signal strength: UWB sends a 2 ns pulse and measures when it comes back;
1 ns of timing error is 30 cm, which is why the DW1000 timestamps to ~15 ps.
▸ Two-way ranging cancels clocks: tag sends, anchor replies after a known delay, tag times the
round trip — neither side needs a synchronized clock, only a stable one.
▸ Antenna delay is the calibration: the chip timestamps at the transceiver, but the signal

spends extra nanoseconds in the PCB trace and antenna; that fixed delay is subtracted per
module and is why uncalibrated modules read 30–50 cm long.
▸ Geometry sets the error: three anchors in a line cannot tell which side of the line you are

on; spread them around the volume and the same ranging error gives a far smaller position
error (dilution of precision).
▸ Multipath is the indoor enemy: a pulse that bounces off a metal shelf arrives late and reads
long; the DW1000 reports first-path power so you can reject ranges that came in via a wall.
## key design decisions

→ Why UWB instead of WiFi or BLE RSSI positioning?: RSSI varies 10 dB with a body in the way,

which is metres of error; UWB time-of-flight is physics-limited to centimetres and is what
every commercial indoor RTLS uses.
→ Why trilaterate on the laptop instead of on the tag?: you want to see every raw range,

residual and rejected measurement while you learn it; moving the solver onto the tag is a
one-evening port once it works.
→ Why three anchors first, then four?: three is the minimum for a 2D fix and forces you to

understand the geometry; the fourth anchor introduces redundancy and residuals — the thing
that makes a real system trustworthy.

## build steps

1
Step 1

Flash three ESP32 + DW1000 boards (Makerfabs ESP32-UWB or a DWM1000 on a breakout) as
anchors at known coordinates — tape measure them to the centimetre, corners of a 4 m × 4
m square, 1.5 m high — and one as a tag.

2
Step 2

Implement (or run) double-sided two-way ranging between the tag and each anchor in turn,
and read the raw distance at 1 m, 2 m and 4 m against a tape — expect a fixed offset of
tens of centimetres.

3
Calibrate antenna delay

adjust the per-module delay constant until all three anchors read within ±5 cm at a known
2 m — this single number is where most of the error lives.

4
Trilaterate on the laptop

three circles, least-squares intersection (solve the linearized 2×2 system), plot the
tag position live over serial at 10 Hz, and watch it jitter when you stand between the
tag and an anchor.

5
Step 5

Walk a 2 m square holding the tag and log the trace; overlay it on the true square and
report RMS error — then add a fourth anchor and show how the residual tells you when one
range is wrong.

You just built the electronics stack of a real
aircraft.

Strip any commercial drone down and it is these six things: an IMU feeding a control loop,
three-phase motor drive, a radio link, a stabilized payload, a battery that reports on itself,
and a way to know where the aircraft is. Every project here is one of those blocks, built
small enough to finish on a bench and real enough to put in an airframe.

None of them are toy demos. Each one maps to a line in a drone-company job posting, and each
one leaves you with a log file, a scope capture, a photo of the board, and a failure you
diagnosed yourself — the four things a technical interviewer actually wants to see.
// the skill ladder
IMU + control loops → three-phase motor drive → RF link budgets → sensor fusion → battery
management → system-level flight test
THE RULES, EVERY SINGLE TIME

Props off for every bench test. A motor that spins up by accident with a propeller on it
is the single most common way people get hurt on these builds — remove the props before
you power anything.

Keep a current-limited bench supply between you and any new board until you have
measured its idle draw; a reversed rail or a shorted MOSFET should pop a limit, not a
battery.

Never charge, balance or discharge a LiPo unattended, and never below 3.0 V per cell — a
puffed pack goes in a fireproof bag outdoors, not back on the bench.
